# Design system

A discipline module — owns the design system's rules, not any one
framework's component syntax. Combine with whichever stack conventions
skill matches the current repo — `react-conventions`,
`angular-conventions`, or a native/mobile stack skill if the design
system covers those too. They ship into a repo as
`.claude/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` and `.cursor/rules/<id>.mdc`.

## What we know about the client's design system

Sourced from the client's rules catalog (version 2.3.1, 2026-08-14).
The ten design-system rules — five web, five mobile — are imported
verbatim by `spine import-rules` into `references/rules/web/` and
`references/rules/mobile/` and listed in the generated block at the end
of this file; what follows is the map of what they cover, so you know
which reference to open and what never to invent.

The design system is called **GV DS** and has two implementations.

**Web** (five entries): a **three-layer token pipeline**;
**Vanilla Extract** theming with a `themeVars` contract, defined token
groups and a **no-raw-values** rule; **multi-brand** theming through a
`DesignSystemProvider`, with brand types, dark/light mode and a brand
identity matrix; **WCAG 2.2 AA** — note 2.2, one level newer than the
2.1 AA baseline the audit checklist below still uses — with ARIA
patterns, keyboard navigation, focus management and `vitest-axe`; and an
MCP tooling workflow built on **Storybook MCP**, with explicit
**never-invent rules for props, icons and tokens** plus CI quality gates.

**Mobile** (five entries): Flutter/Dart with **Atomic Design** layers, a
defined component anatomy and public API exports; a token pipeline
around a **`GvDesignSystem` singleton** with colour-token helpers, font
presets and spacing/border-radius enums, and the same no-hardcode rule;
multi-brand token loading and brand-mode switching through that
singleton; accessibility via the Semantics widget, focus management,
contrast and screen-reader support; and **Widgetbook** use cases with
widget tests, **golden tests** and CI quality gates.

Two things to carry from this: the never-invent rule for props, icons
and tokens is the client's own, already written down in
`references/rules/web/mcp_and_tooling.md` — this module is not
introducing it — and the web side's accessibility target is WCAG 2.2 AA
(`references/rules/web/accessibility.md`), so treat the 2.1 AA checklist
in `references/ui-audit-checklist.md` as a floor, not the target.

## The design system is the source of truth for tokens, not the repo

- Color, spacing, typography, and elevation values come from the
  design system's tokens — never a hardcoded hex/px value in component
  code, even one that happens to match a token's value
- If a token doesn't exist for what's needed, that's a design-system
  gap to raise with `#design-systems-guild`, not a reason to hardcode
  a one-off value

## Component reuse over recreation

- Before building any UI element — button, input, modal, table,
  form field — check the design system's component library first.
  This is the single most common convention break: a custom-built
  component where a design-system one already exists
- If the design system's component is close but not quite right,
  check whether it supports the needed variant/prop before assuming a
  custom build is necessary

## Two live sources, and which one answers which question

When either is connected, prefer it over a static written description —
designs and component libraries change, a skill file describing them
goes stale.

Both tools' Figma integrations expose the same capabilities under
different tool names, so reach for them **by capability** rather than by
a name this file could get wrong:

- **Design context for a node** — the structure, layout, styles and any
  designer annotations for a specific frame. The primary call; always
  make it before writing style or layout code for that screen.
- **Variables and token definitions** — the current token values on that
  file, rather than assuming this document's list is exhaustive.
- **Code-connect mapping** — the component-to-code mapping already
  established for this client, rather than guessing which code component
  a design component corresponds to.
- **Component search across the design system** — whether a component
  already exists, before treating a design as needing a new one built.
- **Screenshot of a node** — for *validating* the built result against
  the design. Never as a token source; a picture is not a hex value.

**Storybook MCP is the second live source**, and where the client's own
design-system package is in play it is the *authoritative* one for the
code contract. The split the client already draws:

| Question | Which source answers it |
|---|---|
| Visual hierarchy, layout, spacing intent, copy | Figma |
| Which component to import, and its allowed props | Storybook / design-system MCP |
| A component's variants and states | Storybook / design-system MCP |
| An icon or an asset | Storybook / design-system MCP |
| Which token exists for a style you need | Storybook / design-system MCP |
| Final check | Figma for visual fidelity, the design system for the technical contract |

If neither is available in a session, fall back to the versioned
documentation of the design-system package the repo actually declares,
and note the gap. Do not infer a component's API from how it looks in
Figma — that is the specific failure the never-invent rule exists to
prevent.

### When the design system does not cover the design

A gap between what a design asks for and what the design system offers
is reported, not closed. Say which component, prop, variant, token or
asset is missing; recommend a contribution to the design system where
the case is reusable; and wait for a decision before implementing a
local alternative. Silently building a one-off is how a design system
stops being one.

## UI work needs a design reference before it needs code

The client's rule, and it is a hard stop rather than a preference: a
task that builds or modifies UI does not start until there is an exact
design reference — a frame URL or a node id — recorded on the ticket or
the task itself. No reference means no code, no stubs, no placeholders;
ask for it and wait.

A task counts as UI work when it touches component, style or markup
files, or when its description mentions screens, layouts, components,
styles, animations or tokens.

Two consequences the client learned the hard way: a screenshot pasted
into a conversation is visual reference only and is **never** a token
source, and silence from the requester is not permission to proceed
without one.

The full extraction protocol — parsing the reference, what to pull out
of the design context call, and how token values map to CSS variables,
utility classes or a theme object — is in
`references/figma-extraction-protocol.md`. What a design handoff owes an
implementer, and how implemented routes are checked back against the
designs, is in `references/design-handoff.md`.

## Accessibility

- Every interactive element has a discernible accessible name — not
  relying on visual context alone
- Color is never the only signal for state (error, success, disabled)
  — pair it with an icon, text, or pattern change
- Focus order follows visual/logical order; nothing interactive is
  keyboard-unreachable

## When reviewing

Flag a custom-built UI element where a design-system component already
covers the case — this is a design-system violation, not a style
preference, and should be treated with the same weight as a stack
convention violation.

Review by lens rather than "looking at it generally" — a general look
finds the thing you happened to notice. The six lenses:

1. **Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA)** — contrast, visible focus, keyboard
   reachability, touch targets, labels and alternative text, heading
   semantics and focus order.
2. **Token and design-system consistency** — colors, type, spacing, and
   components coming from the system, with no magic values outside it.
3. **Visual hierarchy** — the primary action is the emphasized one;
   grouping, alignment, and information density hold up.
4. **States** — every data-bearing view has an empty state, an error
   state, and a loading state; forms have disabled and validation
   states. This is the lens that catches the most real defects and the
   one most often skipped, because the happy path is what got built.
5. **Responsive** — behaviour at the relevant breakpoints, with no
   overflow and no content or action lost on a small screen.
6. **Microcopy** — clear, actionable text, consistent tone and language,
   useful error messages, no leftover placeholder text.

Classify every finding, using these three words — `pr-review` consumes
them directly:

- **Blocking** — a WCAG AA failure on a primary flow, a critical action
  with no error state, or a direct contradiction of the design system.
- **Major** — must be fixed in the next iteration: a visible token
  inconsistency, confusing hierarchy, a broken breakpoint on a secondary
  view.
- **Minor** — worth doing, never blocking on its own.

Each finding cites the lens, the file or view, and the location, with an
actionable recommendation. "The UI could be better" is not a finding.

### Never state a contrast ratio you did not compute

Name the color pair and the tool that measured it, and report the
measured value — or mark the pair unverified and say which tool would
settle it. Never write a ratio, or a pass/fail verdict, from
inspection. The legacy skill this checklist came from shipped two
fabricated ratios, one of them inverting the verdict on a pair that
actually fails AA. In a regulated context a confident wrong
accessibility number is a compliance artifact, which is worse than an
acknowledged gap.

The same rule holds for the rest of the accessibility lens: an
automated checker and a screen-reader pass establish things reading the
code cannot. Say what you checked and how.

### With no design-system reference available

If there is no token source in session — no Figma access, no component
library documentation — do not assume a "correct" palette or type
scale. Restrict the consistency lens to internal consistency between
views, mark what you could not verify `[PENDING]`, and say so in the
verdict. A clean pass on tokens you had no way to check is worse than
no verdict at all.

The full per-component checklist — buttons, inputs, cards, navigation,
modals, interaction states, transitions, breakpoints, and the
verification tools to use — is in `references/ui-audit-checklist.md`.
